Blessedness
BLES-ed-nes
n.
From blessed (Old English bletsian, “to consecrate with blood”) + -ness. Renders the Greek makariotēs, “blessedness, happy state,” and the Hebrew ’esher, “happiness, blessedness,” usually in the plural ’ashrē, “O the happinesses of...”

📖 Biblical Definition

Blessedness, in Scripture, is the deep, settled, God-given state of well-being that belongs to those who stand in the favor of God—not the surface happiness of pleasant circumstances, but the deep happiness of being right with God, walking in His ways, and standing in His covenant favor regardless of outward circumstance. The Psalter opens with the keynote: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly—blessed there is plural in the Hebrew, an exclamation: O the blessednesses of the man! Christ inaugurates His own teaching with a cascade of blessednesses: Blessed are the poor in spirit... Blessed are they that mourn... Blessed are the meek... Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness... Blessed are the merciful... Blessed are the pure in heart... Blessed are the peacemakers... Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness’ sake. The Beatitudes invert the world’s rankings: the blessedness Christ pronounces falls on those the world counts unfortunate (the poor, the mournful, the meek, the hungering, the persecuted) precisely because the inward state that meets the world’s pity in the kingdom’s economy meets the Father’s favor. Blessedness is therefore not a circumstance but a state, not a feeling but a standing, not what the man has but what the man is before God. Romans 4 takes up the same word in justification: David also describeth the blessedness of the man unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works, saying, Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. The deepest blessedness is the blessedness of imputed righteousness: the sinner counted righteous in Christ stands in a blessedness no providence can take away, no enemy can touch, no circumstance can erode. The Beatitude register pulls back the curtain on this same blessedness in its practical fruits: the man Christ counts blessed is the man whose inward state has been shaped by the gospel into the conformity to Christ that is itself a foretaste of the consummated blessedness of seeing God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BLESSEDNESS as happiness; felicity; heavenly joys; the favor of God; in a high sense, the blessed estate of those who are justified and reconciled to God.

expand to see more

BLESSEDNESS, n. — 1. Happiness; felicity; heavenly joys; the favor of God. Where is then the blessedness ye spake of? (Gal 4:15). 2. The blessed estate of those who are justified and reconciled to God; the felicity of saints and angels in heaven.

BLESSED, ppr. — Made happy or prosperous; rendered favorable; consecrated; pronounced happy; in the highest sense, made eternally blessed, as the saints in heaven.

📖 Key Scripture

Psalm 1:1-2 — "Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful. But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night."

Matthew 5:3 — "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

Romans 4:6-8 — "Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works, Saying, Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin."

Revelation 22:14 — "Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Blessedness is corrupted by the prosperity-gospel reduction that equates it with material flourishing and pleasant circumstances, and by the inverse therapeutic flattening that empties the word to mean only subjective well-feeling rather than the standing-in-God’s-favor that Scripture means.

expand to see more

The prosperity-gospel reduction empties blessedness of its biblical depth by re-identifying it with material flourishing and pleasant circumstances. The blessed man, on this account, is the one whose health is excellent, whose finances are abundant, whose family is intact, whose career is ascending. Scripture refuses the substitution at every turn. Christ pronounces blessing precisely on those the world counts unfortunate: the poor in spirit, the mournful, the meek, the persecuted. Paul, sitting in a Roman prison facing execution, writes the most joy-saturated epistle of his career. The man counted by God to be righteous in Christ is blessed even when his body is wasting, his comforts are stripped, and his earthly future is closed; the man whose only blessing is material flourishing is, by Scripture’s judgment, the most pitiable of all (Luke 6:24-26 reverses Christ’s blessings with a corresponding set of woes precisely upon the materially comfortable who have received their reward). Recover the biblical depth, and blessedness recovers its substance: a standing-in-God’s-favor that no providence can erode.

The therapeutic flattening is the contemporary American substitute: blessedness reduced to feeling blessed—the subjective well-feeling that one’s life is going well, that one has things to be grateful for, that the day has gone smoothly. The vocabulary survives; the substance has evaporated. The Bible’s blessedness is objective before it is subjective: the man counted righteous in Christ is blessed whether he feels it or not, and the man whose subjective sense of well-being is high but whose standing before God is unjust is not blessed at all in the biblical sense. The recovery is the recovery of the objective category: blessedness is what one is before God, anchored in imputed righteousness, expressed in the Spirit-wrought Beatitude virtues, and consummated in the seeing-God of the pure in heart. Subjective gratitude is its proper fruit, not its substance; circumstances are its incidental setting, not its definition; the standing-in-God’s-favor that comes by grace through faith in Christ alone is its inalienable root.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek makariotēs (blessedness) and makarios (blessed); Hebrew ’esher / ’ashrē (happiness, blessedness, “O the happinesses!”)—the deep, settled, God-given state of well-being that belongs to those standing in His favor in Christ.

expand to see more

Greek makarios (G3107) — blessed, happy (the Beatitude word; James 1:12, 25; Rev 1:3; 14:13; 16:15; 19:9; 20:6; 22:7, 14).

Greek makariotēs (G3108) — blessedness (Rom 4:6, 9; Gal 4:15).

Hebrew ’esher / ’ashrē (H835) — happiness, blessedness; the exclamatory plural opening Ps 1, 32, 41, 112, 119, 128.

Hebrew bārak (H1288) — to bless (the related verb, of pronouncing or conferring blessing).

Usage

"Blessedness is objective before it is subjective—a standing in God’s favor, not a feeling about one’s circumstances."

"The Beatitudes invert the world’s rankings: the blessed are those the world counts unfortunate, because the inward states the gospel produces are the very things the Father’s favor rests upon."

"Prosperity-gospel reduction equates blessedness with material flourishing; therapeutic flattening reduces it to well-feeling—both miss the standing-in-Christ that is its substance."
